chapters.title: Chapter 4: Dilution, Down Rounds and Protecting Your Stake

lessons.title: Pro-Rata Rights: When to Defend Your Ownership and When to Let Go

children.text: The email arrives on a Tuesday: "We are pleased to share that we have signed a term sheet for our Series A. As an existing investor, you have the right to participate pro-rata. Please confirm your allocation within 15 days." You invested ₹5 lakh at seed. Your pro-rata allocation is ₹10 lakh. Do you write the cheque? This lesson explains what pro-rata rights are, how to calculate your allocation, and a practical framework for deciding when to defend your stake and when to let dilution happen.

body.text: A pro-rata right lets you buy enough of each new round to keep your percentage. It is an option, not an obligation. The best angels use it selectively, doubling down on clear winners and letting the rest dilute.

children.text: What a Pro-Rata Right Is
A
pro-rata right
lets you invest in a future round in proportion to your current ownership. If you own 1% of the company and it raises ₹10 crore, you can put in up to ₹10 lakh on the same terms as the new investor.

markDefs.definition: A contractual right for an existing investor to buy a share of a new funding round equal to their current fully diluted ownership, so their percentage is not diluted.

body.latex: \text{Pro-rata allocation} = \text{Your fully diluted ownership} \times \text{New round size}
body.caption: Buying exactly this much keeps your percentage unchanged, before any ESOP top-up

body.title: Doesn't company law already give me this right?

children.text: Partly. Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a rights issue to be offered to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holdings. But startups usually raise money through a preferential allotment under Section 62(1)(c), approved by special resolution, which is not offered to everyone.

That means your practical pro-rata right almost always comes from the shareholders' agreement and the Articles of Association, usually as a pre-emptive right clause. If it is not written there, assume you do not have it.
Worked Example: Imran and GharSeva

GharSeva Home Services Private Limited is a fictional Hyderabad startup that books verified plumbers, electricians and carpenters through an app. Imran, a Hyderabad software architect, invested ₹5 lakh at seed at ₹100 per share, receiving 5,000 shares. After the seed round, GharSeva has 5,00,000 fully diluted shares, so Imran owns 1%.

Notice how quickly the allocation grows. The Series A pro-rata is twice Imran's original cheque, and the Series B pro-rata is ten times it. Keeping a 1% stake in a successful company gets expensive fast, which is why very few angels can follow on in every round.

stats.label: Never follows on
stats.context: After Series B, with ₹5 lakh invested

body.title: Your allocation
body.prompt: You own 2.5% of a startup on a fully diluted basis. It is raising a ₹16 crore Series A. What is your full pro-rata allocation, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 2.5% × ₹16 crore = ₹40 lakh. If the round also includes an ESOP pool top-up in the pre-money, even investing your full pro-rata will leave you slightly below 2.5%.

children.text: Does Following On Pay Off? It Depends on the Outcome
Here is what each of Imran's strategies returns in three different futures. For simplicity, the modest sale ignores liquidation preferences, which Chapter 5 adds back in.

body.caption: Three strategies, three outcomes (₹ lakh, rounded)

body.title: Profit or loss by strategy (₹ lakh)

children.text: Three lessons jump out:
Follow-on money earns a lower multiple.
Series B money at ₹3,200 per share returns 5x in the big exit. Seed money at ₹100 returns 160x. You are paying a higher price for lower risk.
But it can still add the most rupees.
In the big exit, following both rounds adds ₹390 lakh of profit over never following on.
In a disappointing outcome, following on can hurt.
In the modest sale, the heaviest follow-on strategy makes the least profit, and in a shutdown it loses thirteen times more than the original cheque.

body.text: The decision is not "is this a good company?" but "is this company now clearly better than the other ways I could use this money?" You have something new investors do not: months or years of watching the founders operate. Use that information advantage, and do not follow on out of loyalty alone.

children.text: A Framework for Deciding

body.title: Exercise your pro-rata vs let it go

columns.label: Lean towards exercising when
points: The company is beating its plan on revenue, retention or unit economics
A strong, independent lead investor is setting the price
The founders have kept you well informed, so your view is well grounded
The step-up in price is justified by real progress
The follow-on keeps this company within your concentration limit

columns.label: Lean towards letting go when
points: The round is a down round or a bridge to buy time
Existing institutional investors are not following on themselves
Investor updates have been sparse or evasive
The allocation would make one startup too large a part of your portfolio
You would be investing out of loyalty or fear of missing out

body.label: A common angel rule of thumb
body.context: Many experienced angels set aside a meaningful share of their startup budget, often somewhere between a third and a half, for follow-on rounds in their best-performing companies. The exact ratio varies, but having no reserve at all means you can never use your pro-rata rights when it counts.

body.text: Watch the signalling. When existing VCs with pro-rata rights decline to invest in a new round, new investors notice, and so should you. There can be innocent reasons, such as a fund reaching the end of its investment period, but always ask why insiders are not participating before you commit more.

children.text: How Pro-Rata Works in Practice

body.title: Exercising a pro-rata right (a typical sequence)

events.title: Term sheet signed
events.description: The company agrees terms with a lead investor, including the total round size and how much is reserved for existing investors.

events.title: Pre-emption notice
events.description: The company sends existing investors a notice with the price, instrument and each holder's pro-rata allocation.

events.title: Response window
events.description: You typically have a fixed window, often 15 to 30 days, to confirm how much you will take. Silence usually counts as a no.

events.title: Documents and funds
events.description: You sign the share subscription documents and transfer funds. NRIs investing on a repatriation basis also need FEMA compliance.

events.title: Allotment
events.description: The company allots shares and files Form PAS-3. Check your holding matches the allocation you paid for.

children.text: Major investor thresholds.
Many agreements give pro-rata rights only to investors above a minimum stake or cheque size. A ₹5 lakh direct angel may not qualify.
Syndicates and angel funds.
If you invested through a syndicate or SEBI-registered angel fund, the vehicle holds the pro-rata right. The lead decides whether to offer a follow-on, and you usually commit fresh money to it.
Cut-backs.
In a hot round, the lead investor may want more of the round and push existing investors to take less than their full pro-rata. Strong contracts limit this.
Super pro-rata.
Some early investors negotiate the right to take more than their pro-rata share, letting them increase their stake in later rounds.

body.title: Which one would you pass on?
body.question: You hold pro-rata rights in four startups. Which follow-on is the weakest case for investing?
options: An up round led by a respected new VC after revenue tripled in a year
A bridge round at a flat price after the company missed its plan, with both existing VCs declining to participate
A Series A where your allocation is 5% of your startup budget and monthly updates show strong retention
A Series B at a 3x step-up where you have watched the founders hit every milestone they promised
body.explanation: A flat bridge after a missed plan, with the best-informed institutional investors declining, combines weak performance with negative signalling. The other three combine real progress with good information and reasonable position sizing.

body.title: More than your share
body.textWithBlank: The right to invest more than your proportionate share of a future round, and so increase your ownership, is called a super ___ right.
body.explanation: Super pro-rata rights are usually negotiated by early lead investors and are uncommon for small angels.

body.title: Imran's Series B decision
body.scenario: GharSeva's Series B notice arrives. Imran's full pro-rata is ₹50 lakh at ₹3,200 per share. His total startup budget is ₹1.5 crore across 12 companies, and he has already put ₹15 lakh into GharSeva. The company has grown revenue 2.5x in a year and the round is led by a well-known growth fund. Both seed and Series A VCs are taking their full pro-rata.
body.prompt: Should Imran take his full ₹50 lakh? What are his options?
body.modelAnswer:
The company signals are strong: real growth, a quality new lead and full insider participation. But the full ₹50 lakh is a portfolio construction problem.

1. Concentration. ₹15 lakh plus ₹50 lakh would put ₹65 lakh, over 43% of his ₹1.5 crore budget, into one startup. A single bad outcome would wreck the portfolio.
2. Lower multiple. Series B money at ₹3,200 needs a much larger exit to earn the returns his seed money can.

Better options:
1. Take a partial allocation, for example ₹15 to ₹20 lakh, keeping GharSeva to around 20% to 25% of his budget.
2. Check whether a secondary component lets him sell a small part of his seed shares at a good price to fund some of the follow-on without adding new money.
3. Confirm the terms: same CCPS series and rights as the new lead, and whether any ESOP top-up sits in the pre-money.
4. Decide in advance how he would handle a Series C pro-rata, which could be even larger.

Following on is sensible. Following on in full is not.

body.title: Before you exercise a pro-rata right
steps: Confirm the right exists in the shareholders' agreement or Articles, and whether you meet any major investor threshold.
Calculate your full allocation: fully diluted ownership × round size.
Review the latest metrics against the plan you invested on.
Find out who is leading, at what price, and whether existing institutional investors are participating.
Check the instrument, liquidation preference and anti-dilution terms of the new series.
Test the position against your concentration limit and follow-on reserve.
Diarise the response deadline so silence does not decide for you.

cards.definition: The right to invest in a new round in proportion to your current ownership, to avoid being diluted.
Your fully diluted ownership multiplied by the new round size.
The contractual clause, usually in the shareholders' agreement, that gives existing investors first right to new shares.
A minimum stake or investment required before an investor receives pro-rata or information rights.
A right to invest more than your proportionate share of a future round.
The negative message sent to new investors when insiders decline to follow on.
Money an angel sets aside to invest in later rounds of their best-performing startups.

points: Pro-rata allocation = your fully diluted ownership × new round size.
In Indian startups, pro-rata rights usually come from the shareholders' agreement, not from company law.
Allocations grow fast: keeping 1% through a Series B can cost many times your original cheque.
Follow-on money earns a lower multiple but can add the most rupees in a strong outcome, and loses the most in a failure.
Exercise selectively: back real progress, good information and reasonable position sizes; pass on weak signals and over-concentration.
Keep a follow-on reserve and watch for major investor thresholds, syndicate structures and response deadlines.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. GharSeva and the investors described are fictional. Exit values shown are illustrative, and the modest sale ignores liquidation preferences. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
